items.title: FOL-Proof: Verifying LLM Text-to-Logic Translations via Deterministic Semantics
items.summary: Large Language Models (LLMs) are increasingly used to translate natural-language statements into first-order logic (FOL) to improve reasoning. However, LLMs are prone to errors, and so a semantically unfaithful FOL formula could corrupt downstream reasoning. We present FOL-Proof, a semantic firewall pipeline that validates LLM-generated FOL translations against independently derived linguistic interpretations. FOL-Proof operates by deterministically obtaining a pool of candidate translations via semantic analysis tools, such as the English Resource Grammar and Minimal Recursion Semantics; then applying an SMT solver to check each derived reading for logical equivalence to the LLM-generated formula. If the translation is faithful it is accepted; otherwise, it is rejected, or optionally repaired via repeated invocations to the LLM. The procedure is conservative: incomplete search, unsupported constructions, or inconclusive checks yield abstention rather than false rejection. We evaluated FOL-Proof on established benchmarks (ProofWriter, RuleTaker and PrOntoQA), and also on a new adversarial benchmark (LongFaithCheck). Our experiments show that FOL-Proof attains near perfect selective accuracy, while direct LLM judges and round-trip baselines show substantially worse performance.

items.title: Towards Realistic Evaluation of Uncertainty Quantification for LLM-Based Recommender Systems
items.summary: Large language models (LLMs) provide a flexible interface for recommendation systems. However, their issued rankings require reliable instance-level uncertainty monitoring. In this scenario, comparing uncertainty quantification (UQ) methods becomes challenging because LLM rankers lack a standard item-classification head. Their scores may depend on option labels, prompts, generation procedures, and the available user and item evidence. Existing methods derive uncertainty from different sources and apply it at different stages of the recommendation process. Some methods evaluate an issued ranking, whereas others use uncertainty to change the ranking itself, making direct comparison difficult. Here we introduce a fixed-ranking benchmark which evaluates eight heterogeneous UQ signals as record-level monitors under a shared output contract. We evaluate these signals across four recommendation datasets and two LLM backbones under a shared fixed-ranking protocol. From the results, we draw three main observations. First, UQ method ordering changes across backbones even on the same reference instances. Second, ranking-aligned Top10Mass provides the strongest scalar Error@10 detection in several evaluation conditions, reflecting effective cutoff-aligned monitoring, while its advantage narrows for popularity-tail targets. Third, scalar UQ signals are weak at identifying which control has the larger clipped NDCG@10 difference, whereas source-specific signals, including Perturbation Rank Instability and simple listwise distances, provide stronger paired-control agreement, reflecting their sensitivity to the two controlled evidence sources. These findings motivate us to evaluate ranking-failure detection, robustness across recommendation conditions, and responses to controlled evidence changes as distinct properties of UQ.

items.title: LatentLens: Rethinking Latent Interface in Multi-Agent Systems
items.summary: Latent interfaces let agents in a multi-agent system communicate through continuous representations rather than decoded text. Prior work reports performance and efficiency gains, but neither separates latent communication from the agent harness nor examines its internal components, leaving its actual contribution unclear. We propose LatentLens, a framework that decouples the latent interface at two levels: externally from the agent harness, to measure its contribution to overall performance (RQ1), and internally into realignment compatibility, information accessibility, and propagation dynamics, to identify the benefits and limitations of each (RQ2). Across seven benchmarks with Qwen3 models, adding the latent interface to the same harness does not improve and can even substantially degrade accuracy. Internally, latent representations retain some domain information, but incompatible realignment can substantially degrade performance, and repeated latent steps can amplify representation-level failures. Thus, while latent representations may preserve information, they do not necessarily ensure effective communication, which also requires compatible realignment, information accessibility, and stable propagation.

items.title: Introducing Search for Agents
items.summary: Flip one toggle to make your site searchable by AI agents — complete with automatic content indexing, a discoverable search API, and native HTTP QUERY support.
items.content_excerpt: AI Search , our service that indexes your content and lets you add search to any application or agent without having to build an entire retrieval infrastructure, has supported adding your website as a data source for a while now, automatically crawling, converting and indexing its pages. Still, setting up an AI Search instance for your website requires manually creating and configuring it initially, and then doing all the integration work to get the search endpoints available from your domain and to make sure that agents know where to find the index and know how to use it. Today we're introducing Search for Agents , which puts that setup behind a toggle in your Cloudflare dashboard. Turn it on for your zone, and our service will create your AI Search instance, start indexing your content, and make search discoverable and available from your own domain. The idea follows naturally from Markdown for Agents , where Cloudflare's network converts any HTML page to Markdown in real time for enabled zones using content negotiation headers. Similarly, Search for Agents leverages the power of AI Search by automatically creating an index for your zone and exposing APIs that any AI agent can discover and use to search your website, under your domain, all done at the network level. You can enable Search for Agents using the API, or by going to the dashboard in your zone page, under Quick Actions : Search for Agents is available to all customers, including Free (with limits ). Once it’s enabled, Cloudflare will automatically create an AI Search instance, start crawling and indexing the content in your zone. Refer to our developer documentation to understand how the crawling process works. You can access your instance directly from this page, or by going to directly to your account’s AI > AI Search instances view: The AI Search instance for your zone is created with default settings, but you can enable reranking or change configuration options like cache settings at any time. Refer to our documentation for the full list of options. Once AI Search indexes your content, you or any agent on the Internet can start using Search for Agents, subject to your domain settings (e.g. your bot management settings, AI Crawl Control and web application firewall ( WAF ) configurations). Search isn't much use if the agents don’t know it's there. To facilitate discoverability, Search for Agents automatically advertises the search endpoint on every page of your site. items.title: Ten MCP Servers, Still Too Little Context | Birgitta Boeckeler
items.summary:
Context engineering starts with admitting that not all context is the same. Birgitta Boeckeler, now a principal engineer at Unblocked after almost 14 years at Thoughtworks, splits it into codified context you author and ambient context your agents pull from the environment, and explains why each needs its own delivery lifecycle.

Watch all the AI DevCon NYC 2026 talks:
https://tessl.co/p7w

Recorded live at AI DevCon NYC 2026, Simon Maple sits down with Birgitta to dig into why ten MCP servers can still leave an agent with too little context, how a context engine settles a conflict between a Slack thread and a README (often by checking the code), and when ambient knowledge should be promoted into a skill. Then stay for her full DevCon talk, Context != Context: One Window, Different Lifecycles, on what it takes to ingest, evaluate, assemble and observe ambient context.

What we cover:
– Codified vs ambient context, and why they need different delivery mechanisms
– Security and permissions when agents read and post organizational context
– Why MCP servers can leave an agent with too little context
– How context conflicts get resolved: recency, the code and an expert graph
– When ambient context should become a skill, and how to evaluate a context engine
– Birgitta's AI DevCon talk: a context engineering lifecycle for ambient context

Chapters:
00:00:00 - Introduction
00:03:56 - Security and permissions in a context layer
00:07:04 - Context != context: codified vs ambient context
00:10:58 - Organizational context and code as a source of reality
00:13:18 - Signal to noise: too much context, or too little
00:16:10 - Where organizational context helps most
00:19:04 - How a context engine resolves conflicting context
00:21:32 - When ambient context should become a skill
00:25:30 - Fixing repeated agent mistakes: guidance or sensors

items.title: Skip the DRAM Tier: MoRI UMBP Runs the Agentic KV Cache on NVMe
items.summary: On AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs, a MoRI UMBP KV pool on NVMe matched a DRAM pool of the same size within 1% for Kimi-K3 on vLLM, and drives that hold a day of agent KV cost less than DRAM that holds 31 minutes.
items.story_key: story|title:skip the dram tier mori umbp runs the agentic kv cache on nvme
items.content_excerpt: Most of the traffic in agentic serving is multi-turn sessions that resend long prefixes. In the AgentX benchmark replaying real Claude Code sessions, the median turn is 142K input tokens, and over 96% of those tokens are a prefix the server has already seen [3] . A KV cache hit means the prefill node only has to process the small delta. A miss forces a full recomputation of the prefix, which burns GPU time and delays the first token. In our 42 runs of Kimi-K3 on vLLM, raising the KV cache hit rate by 1% of prompt tokens, for example from 95% to 96%, was worth about 10% more throughput (Figure 3). A KV cache hit needs the session’s prefix to still be in memory when its next turn arrives. With dozens of sessions open at once, memory runs out. GPU memory goes first, and host DRAM is the usual next tier. But DRAM fills too: Kimi-K3 wrote 2.3 to 4.6 TB of KV to the pool an hour in our runs, so a 1.8 TB DRAM pool, which lists at about $76,000, holds only the last 23 to 47 minutes of it. That led us to a simple question: why not skip the DRAM tier and put vLLM’s KV pool straight on NVMe? We tried it on AMD Instinct™ MI355X GPUs with UMBP, the KV cache pool in AMD’s open-source MoRI library. At the same size, NVMe matched DRAM’s throughput within 1% on Kimi-K3, in two sets of runs on different machines (Figure 1). On a second workload with longer prompts, NVMe came within 1% of a DRAM pool of the same size. The NVMe pool has no DRAM tier: DRAM only buffers new KV on its way to the drives and stages reads, about 80 GB against the DRAM pool’s 1.8 TB. And NVMe’s cost follows the KV it writes, not the KV it holds, so drives rated for Kimi-K3’s writes cost less than that DRAM pool and hold a full day of KV. “Agentic workloads keep sessions open for minutes or hours, and their KV cache quickly outgrows GPU memory and host DRAM. Results like these, with NVMe keeping up with DRAM at the same pool size, change how we think about sizing KV cache capacity in AI clusters. We’re glad to see this work done in the open, in vLLM and MoRI.” — Dennis Kennetz, Principal Infrastructure Engineer, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure DeepSeek already keeps agent KV caches on SSD: the deployment notes for its DeepInfer engine describe three days of retention for agent traffic, on about 14.4 TB of SSD per GPU [4] . This work references DeepInfer for the idea of keeping the KV cache on SSD and for two of its techniques, layer-wise loading and bounded replay, which we test on vLLM below. Figure 1.

items.title: vLLM Day-0 Support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview: Plugin Deployment and E2E Inference Acceleration
items.summary: vLLM supports Baidu's ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview on day 0 through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin on the released vllm==0.32.0 wheel, with structure-aware kernel fusion, FlashIndexer, W4A8 QAT and DSpark speculative decoding.
items.story_key: model:vllm|ver:5.5|variant:flash,preview|title:vllm day 0 support for ernie 5 5 flash preview plugin deployment and e2e inferen
items.content_excerpt: The Baidu ERNIE team has worked with vLLM to bring day-0 support for ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview to vLLM. ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview is a sparse mixture-of-experts (MoE) model with 280B total parameters and 14B activated per token. It supports a 1M-token context, thinks before it answers, and uses tool calling to carry out long-horizon Agent tasks. vLLM supports the model on release day through the vLLM-ERNIE plugin, a standalone package that you install into the same environment as the official vllm==0.32.0 wheel. Install the released vLLM wheel and the plugin into the same environment. vLLM discovers the plugin automatically through its vllm.general_plugins entrypoint, so there is nothing to import or configure. The following command serves the default FP4 weights on a single 4-GPU node, with DSpark speculative decoding drafting 7 tokens per step: To turn off thinking for a request, pass "chat_template_kwargs": {"enable_thinking": false} . Launch commands for 1M context, attention TP and PD disaggregation are in the vLLM-ERNIE README and the vLLM recipe . ERNIE 5.5 Flash was designed with inference cost as a primary goal from the start, weighing activated compute, KV cache size and long-context overhead together. Every component, from the attention structure and residual connections to the MoE layers and the output head, was redesigned around that goal. For design and training details, see the ERNIE 5.5 Flash Preview blog . ERNIE 5.5 Flash introduces several new structures in attention and MoE: low-rank cross-head post-mixing (VHA post-mix), Multi-Router Latent MoE, the MultiMax output head and sigmoid output gating. When implemented op by op from their mathematical definitions, these structures produce many intermediate tensors and pay for them in memory traffic and kernel launches. For each structure, we designed a dedicated fused kernel around its compute and memory-access profile, and folded everything that can be precomputed into the weights at load time. The fused kernels run 1.55× to 6.53× faster than naive implementations. Together, these fusions cover the full forward pass of ERNIE 5.5 Flash, from attention and MoE routing to the output head. They cut the number of kernel launches and the round trips of intermediate tensors through GPU memory while keeping the numerics aligned, and they underpin the model's high inference performance. The Baidu ERNIE inference team developed FlashIndexer, a lightweight indexer acceleration built on dynamic head routing

items.title: codex 0.172.0
items.summary:
New Features

  • Follow thread links from search results and transcripts to open saved conversations and nested agents in the terminal. (#62332)
  • Press Tab to complete arguments for supported slash commands. For example, /mcp lo completes to /mcp login. (#62343)
  • Jump between task groups in the agent command center with Shift+Up and Shift+Down. (#62200)
  • Optional stdio MCP servers with cached tool lists now start on their first tool call by default. (#62366)
  • Set an approval reviewer for individual connected app tools in config.toml. (#62360)
  • App-server clients can select Amazon Bedrock Runtime during setup or sign-in. (#62222)

Bug Fixes

  • codex exec resume restores saved sandbox permissions, the working directory, and workspace roots unless explicitly overridden. (#62194)
  • Remote sessions preserve working directories, workspace roots, and writable paths when the client and server run on different operating systems. (#62375, #62376, #62377)
  • Codex reports provider errors as soon as they arrive in a response stream and identifies which API spend limit was reached. (#62329, #62356)
  • Interrupting a parent turn preserves queued replies from child agents for the next turn. (#62348)
  • Use PageUp and PageDown to read and submit answer choices that are taller than the terminal’s answer area. (#62209)
  • Cloud replies that finish after history loads now update in place, keeping the terminal transcript in order. (#62403)

Documentation

  • The bundled openai-docs skill now covers migration to GPT-6.2 Astra and Sol, including endpoint choices and tool-calling requirements. (#62447)

Chores

  • Code Mode now uses gRPC for all host connections. The code_mode_host_grpc setting is deprecated. (#62476)
  • Python formatting and SDK type generation now verify dependency hashes against the repository lockfile. (#62346)

items.title: SpatialCraft: Evolving Procedural Intelligence from Experience and Skills for Spatial Reasoning Agents
items.summary: Spatial reasoning agents increasingly rely on external tools, such as 3D reconstruction, segmentation, and geometric computation, to answer questions that a multimodal large language model (MLLM) cannot resolve from pixels alone. Tool access, however, shifts the bottleneck to orchestration: the agent must decide which tools to call, in what order, and how to interpret their outputs, yet a stateless agent repeats the same mistakes across tasks. We ask whether a frozen tool-using agent can improve its orchestration from its own interaction history, without parameter updates. We present SpatialCraft, a self-evolving framework that maintains two forms of external knowledge: Experiences, condition-action tactics distilled by contrasting rollouts of the same task, and Skills, multi-step procedures with explicit activation and termination conditions. Three designs couple the two streams. Experiences can be anchored to a Skill, appearing only while it is active rather than once per task. A Contrastive Utility Score estimates each Experience's effect by randomly withholding it across rollouts of the same task, separating its contribution from task difficulty, and Experiences with consistently positive utility are consolidated into the Skills they support. Across five spatial benchmarks and four backbones, SpatialCraft achieves the best accuracy in all 20 settings, showing that a frozen agent can learn to orchestrate spatial tools from its own experience.

items.title: LoomKV: Lossless KV Cache Compression from GPU Memory to SSD for LLM Serving
items.summary: Large language model (LLM) serving engines offload the key/value (KV) cache from GPU memory to host DRAM and SSD so multi-turn and agent requests can reuse prompt prefixes. Capacity then limits service at two levels: external tiers govern prefix reuse before eviction, while the GPU KV pool bounds concurrent long requests, and lossy compression alters KV values and outputs. LoomKV brings lossless KV compression to both external tiers (tier mode) and the GPU pool (pool mode) on an unmodified engine. Using a calibrated per-head two-level 3-bit code over BF16 high bytes (sign and upper seven exponent bits), LoomKV stores BF16 KV at 0.71 of its raw size across nine models and FP8 KV at 0.85-0.87. In tier mode, TileStream writes exact-length records with length readback off the load path, leaving tier storage, eviction, and prefetch unchanged, and decompresses fetched records straight into scattered GPU pages. In pool mode, FragPack packs variable-length records into smaller shared-budget GPU pages read in place by a fused decode-attention kernel faster than FlashAttention-3 on BF16. Built with LMCache and vLLM, LoomKV makes compressed tiers act as 1.4x larger raw tiers on AgentX: across LMCache's LRU cliff, tier mode delivers 2.7-3.6x raw's goodput and 1.9-3.1x lower mean time-to-first-token (TTFT), shifts the cliff identically under other simulated replacement policies, and cuts repeated-prompt TTFT up to 1.7x via SSD-to-DRAM promotion. When tiers hold the working set, pool mode fits 1.31-1.34x as many GPU tokens, admitting 12 long requests with roughly raw's queue and goodput at 8. On an AI IDE trace where both tiers and the GPU pool are constrained, tier and pool modes raise goodput by 1.24x and 1.59x. Where raw capacity suffices, compression costs at most 2.2% throughput; tier mode is bit-exact with raw tiers, and pool mode matches FlashAttention-3's numerical accuracy.

items.story_key: story|title:sharing catalog metadata across data platforms engines and agents
items.content_excerpt: Make table and column context accessible for discovery, governance, and agentic workflows. We’re excited to announce support for catalog labels – a new capability in the Apache Iceberg™ REST Catalog API that enables platforms, engines, and agents to access context such as business purpose, ownership and data classifications maintained in Iceberg REST-compatible catalogs. This shared context supports discovery, governance, and agentic workflows across the data and AI ecosystem. We believe that catalog metadata should be as open and portable as the data it describes. As enterprises bring more tools into their open lakehouse architectures, they need a common way to share the context that makes their data understandable, useful, and secure for all teams, regardless of what tools they use. Today, that context often remains siloed in the source catalog. Data and AI teams must recreate classifications across platforms, maintain custom metadata synchronization pipelines, or work with agents that lack complete context. Databricks is joined by Google Cloud, Salesforce, ClickHouse, Atlan, Collibra, DataHub, Immuta, Trust3 AI, PhoenixAI, and Datastrato in advancing this shared vision of metadata interoperability. Catalog labels offer a path toward that vision, making catalog context portable while allowing each platform to retain its own capabilities and controls. Databricks worked with the Apache Iceberg community to add an optional labels field to the Iceberg REST LoadTable response. This gives catalogs a standard way to expose table- and column-level context to other platforms, tools, and agents. Labels are string key-value pairs that can describe business ownership, intended use, sensitivity or other catalog-maintained context. The standard defines a common format for sharing this metadata without prescribing its vocabulary or interpretation, giving each platform the flexibility to build on it in its own way. An authorized data steward assigns domain=customer_support and the Databricks system tag system.certification_status=certified to the table, and content_type=support_case_summary to the issue_summary column. A catalog exposing these tags could include the following in its Iceberg REST LoadTable response: For example, PyIceberg has added support for accessing catalog labels in Python . items.title: Data + AI Anywhere: AlloyDB Omni integration with local models
items.summary:
Open models like Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind are a great option to keep your data local. But how can a local AI model integrate with on-premises data?

AlloyDB Omni, Google’s 100% PostgreSQL-compatible database that runs anywhere, now integrates with locally hosted large language models (LLMs). With AlloyDB Omni, you can build agentic experiences on your own infrastructure and on your own terms. Whether it’s in the cloud, in your datacenter, or even on your laptop, you can have data plus AI anywhere.

Built-in AI for your local environment

AlloyDB Omni is a downloadable, run-anywhere edition of AlloyDB that easily deploys to your own infrastructure, including on-premises. AlloyDB Omni packs powerful, built-in AI, including the same ScaNN indexing technology powering Google Search. When you pair AlloyDB Omni with a model, you can store vector embeddings at scale; search them semantically; and even query the database using natural language. You can use virtually any model you like, whether that’s a frontier Cloud-hosted model like Gemini or a local model. And with locally hosted models you maintain complete control over your data environment.

Connecting to Gemma 4, Qwen3.8, and other local models

You can now connect AlloyDB Omni to local models like Gemma 4 and Qwen3.8. No matter which model you choose, the architecture remains the same.

This setup enables entirely new use cases for environments that were previously blocked from adopting agentic capabilities. If you operate an air-gapped network or have data locality requirements, you can still build intelligent applications. You can analyze local logs, generate summaries of proprietary internal documents, and power localized chatbots—all while maintaining strict data governance.

  • Keep data on-premises: Because the database and the model sit in the same local environment, your data never crosses the public internet.

  • Reduce latency: Processing inference requests locally minimizes network transit time.

  • Query directly via SQL: Your standard database queries can invoke machine learning functions that process data locally. Like this:

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm') AS summary FROM customer_feedback; customer_name | summary ---------------+----------------------------------------------------------------------- Alice | The customer demands a refund for a double charge or they will cancel Bob | The user likes the product but requests dark mode support."), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc6450>)])]>

Next, you’ll see how to run queries like this yourself, step by step.

Get started

You can test this integration on your own machines today. Using a Kubernetes environment we will show you how to deploy and integrate AlloyDB Omni and a local open model.

Step 0: Before you begin

In this example, we will use Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) to host the AlloyDB Omni database and local model. GKE gives us a standardized, reproducible environment but you can use the same setup on-prem or almost anywhere.

We will assume you have already setup:

  1. A GKE cluster, and

  2. Kubernetes tools kubectl and Helm

Step 1: Deploy the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes Operator

We will use the AlloyDB Omni Kubernetes operator to set up our AlloyDB Omni database. The Operator makes deploying and maintaining AlloyDB Omni a breeze.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "helm install \ cert-manager oci://quay.io/jetstack/charts/cert-manager \ --version v1.21.3 \ --namespace cert-manager \ --create-namespace \ --set crds.enabled=true \ --set global.leaderElection.namespace=cert-manager helm install alloydbomni-operator oci://gcr.io/alloydb-omni/alloydbomni-operator \ --version 1.9.0 \ --create-namespace \ --namespace alloydb-omni-system \ $(helm install --help | grep -q -- '--rollback-on-failure' && echo '--rollback-on-failure' || echo '--atomic') \ --timeout 5m"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc4ed0>)])]>

Step 2: Create your AlloyDB Omni database

Don’t forget to enable the googleMLExtension.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl create namespace ai-demo cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: v1 kind: Secret metadata: name: db-pw-my-omni namespace: ai-demo type: Opaque data: my-omni: "VmVyeVN0cm9uZ1Bhc3N3b3Jk" # password "VeryStrongPassword" --- apiVersion: alloydbomni.dbadmin.goog/v1 kind: DBCluster metadata: name: my-omni namespace: ai-demo spec: databaseVersion: "18.4.0" primarySpec: adminUser: passwordRef: name: db-pw-my-omni features: googleMLExtension: enabled: true resources: cpu: 2 memory: 4Gi disks: - name: DataDisk size: 20Gi storageClass: standard dbLoadBalancerOptions: annotations: networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "internal" allowExternalIncomingTraffic: true EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc6e10>)])]>

Step 3: Deploy your AI model

We will use Ollama to help us deploy our model.

In this example we deploy Gemma 4 from Google DeepMind. Or, you can modify this command to deploy Qwen3.8 – just change a few lines as noted in the comments.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'cat << \'EOF\' | kubectl apply -f - apiVersion: apps/v1 kind: Deployment metadata: name: ollama namespace: ai-demo spec: replicas: 1 selector: matchLabels: app: ollama template: metadata: labels: app: ollama spec: containers: - name: ollama image: ollama/ollama:latest ports: - containerPort: 11434 env: - name: OLLAMA_KEEP_ALIVE value: "-1" # keep the model in RAM - name: OLLAMA_LOAD_TIMEOUT value: "20m" resources: requests: cpu: "4" memory: "16Gi" # for Qwen 3.8: 24Gi volumeMounts: - name: models mountPath: /root/.ollama lifecycle: postStart: exec: command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull gemma4:12b) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] # For Qwen 3.8, comment out the line above and use this one: # command: ["/bin/sh", "-c", "(sleep 5 && ollama pull qwen3.8) >/dev/null 2>&1 &"] volumes: - name: models ephemeral: volumeClaimTemplate: spec: accessModes: ["ReadWriteOnce"] resources: requests: storage: 30Gi --- apiVersion: v1 kind: Service metadata: name: ollama-service namespace: ai-demo spec: type: ClusterIP ports: - port: 11434 targetPort: 11434 selector: app: ollama EOF'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc6690>)])]>

Step 4: Register the model with AlloyDB Omni

Connect to your database.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', 'kubectl exec -it -n ai-demo $(kubectl get pod -n ai-demo -l alloydbomni.internal.dbadmin.goog/task-type=database -o jsonpath=\'{.items[0].metadata.name}\') -c database -- env PGPASSWORD="VeryStrongPassword" psql -h 127.0.0.1 -U postgres'), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc68d0>)])]>

Note: If you receive a connection error, you might need to wait a moment for your database to provision.

Now you should be connected to your AlloyDB Omni database with the psql client. Next, run the following SQL script to register your local model.

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS google_ml_integration; ALTER SYSTEM SET google_ml_integration.request_timeout_in_seconds = 600; SELECT pg_reload_conf(); CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform( model_id character varying, prompt text, generation_config json, system_instructions json ) RETURNS json AS $$ SELECT json_build_object( 'model', CASE model_id WHEN 'gemma4_llm' THEN 'gemma4:12b' WHEN 'qwen3_8_llm' THEN 'qwen3.8' END, 'messages', json_build_array( json_build_object('role', 'system', 'content', COALESCE(system_instructions->'systemInstruction'->'parts'->0->>'text', 'You are a helpful assistant.')), json_build_object('role', 'user', 'content', prompt) ) ); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform( model_id character varying, response json ) RETURNS text AS $$ SELECT trim(regexp_replace( response->'choices'->0->'message'->>'content', '<think>.*?</think>', '', 's')); $$ LANGUAGE sql; CALL google_ml.create_model( model_id => 'gemma4_llm', -- and/or 'qwen3_8_llm', model_request_url => 'http://ollama-service.ai-demo.svc.cluster.local:11434/v1/chat/completions', model_provider => 'custom', model_type => 'llm', model_in_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_input_transform', model_out_transform_fn => 'google_ml.ollama_llm_output_transform' );"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc4410>)])]>

Note: If you receive a Resource not found error, wait a moment for the model to load.

In addition to registering your model, the above script tells AlloyDB Omni how to interpret the model’s raw output. In this example chain-of-thought (CoT) reasoning is part of the response inside <think></think> tags. We don’t want the CoT, so our output transform function removes it.

Step 5: Try it out!

You can use functions like ai.generate built-in to AlloyDB Omni to connect to your local model – without ever leaving the SQL client!

code_block
<ListValue: [StructValue([('code', "CREATE TABLE customer_feedback ( id SERIAL PRIMARY KEY, customer_name TEXT, comment TEXT ); INSERT INTO customer_feedback (customer_name, comment) VALUES ('Alice', 'I was charged twice on my credit card! Please refund $49 immediately or I will cancel.'), ('Bob', 'Great product, but can you please add dark mode support?'); SELECT customer_name, ai.generate('Summarize in 1 short sentence: ' || comment, model_id => 'gemma4_llm' /* or 'qwen3_8_llm' */) AS summary FROM customer_feedback;"), ('language', ''), ('caption', <wagtail.rich_text.RichText object at 0x7f5a5ccc7950>)])]>

Make it your own

Try out all the AI features that AlloyDB Omni has to offer! AlloyDB Omni supports fast vector search, built-in AI functions, and more. Give them a try and build something great.

items.title: claude-code v2.1.328
items.summary:
What's changed

  • Added auto mode for Claude Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform, Microsoft Foundry and Claude apps gateway; interactive sessions with no permission mode start in it
  • Added "onFailure": "block" for mcp_tool hooks, as for command and HTTP hooks: a hook whose call fails blocks the action
  • Added a warning when a message from a session that skips permission prompts may be held and dropped by a cloud session
  • Added a notice in /status and claude doctor when an OpenTelemetry exporter has no endpoint and its data would likely be lost
  • Added CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_DEFERRED_TOOL_RESUME, which lets a host stop claude -p --resume and --continue from running a tool call that a hook deferred
  • Added support for apps that embed Claude Code to switch on the policy plugin's allowManagedModsOnly option; an admin's managed settings still win
  • Added a startup warning to the Claude apps gateway when a policy's maxEffortLevel is not a valid effort level
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --repository-folder to name the folder that sessions use for a repository at --capacity 1, in place of its path under the base folder, which can't be a symbolic link
  • Self-hosted runner: Added a start-up warning when the host's settings.json sets a default permission mode that sessions ignore
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --hook-label to claude self-hosted-runner orchestrator, to hand chosen session labels to the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added --metadata key=value to claude --environment, to label a session for the spawn-runner hook
  • Self-hosted runner: Added claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_session_queue_wait_by_reason_seconds to the orchestrator's /metrics, so a re-opened session's wait can be told from a new one's
  • Self-hosted runner: Added an orchestrator metric, claude_code_self_hosted_orchestrator_sessions_given_up_total, that counts by cause how often Anthropic gave up starting a runner for a session
  • Fixed Bash commands in zsh stopping with a "not found" error at a word that starts with =, such as echo ==== or [ a == b ]; =cmd no longer expands to a command's path
  • Fixed automatic compaction reusing the session's earlier system prompt instead of rebuilding it the way /compact does
  • Fixed markdown rendering freezing on some very long or malformed input
  • Fixed rare screen freezes
  • Fixed Esc often being lost at a permission prompt or question when you typed straight after it; in terminals that send Alt as Esc and a key, an unused Alt or Option key now declines there
  • Fixed a paste or a terminal's reply being typed into the prompt when a slow connection cut it in two
  • Fixed saving a scheduled task erasing the project's other saved tasks when the scheduled tasks file can't be read, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed a scheduled task with a typo in the project's scheduled tasks file being deleted the next time that file was saved
  • Fixed a case where a resumed cloud session could lose its compaction summary or recent messages when a message was saved late
  • Fixed the token counts on the spinner and for subagents counting a retried reply twice, missing replies that were not streamed, and standing still while Claude thinks
  • Fixed the error shown when usage credits run out mid-response, which named a rate limit
  • Fixed auto mode failing every turn outside Claude Desktop with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set behind a gateway rejecting betas, on Bedrock, Agent Platform, Foundry or Claude apps gateway
  • Fixed CLAUDE_STREAM_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS not lengthening the 5-minute connection limit on gateways, custom base URLs and cloud providers
  • Fixed some Claude Desktop sessions on third-party providers, other than scheduled tasks, ending for good with "Prompt is too long" after large tool results; the largest are now left out
  • Fixed MCP tools whose input schema starts with anyOf, oneOf or allOf going missing on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Fixed an MCP tool with an invalid input schema failing requests on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off; the tool is now left out and Claude is told why
  • Fixed effort being turned off for a subagent's model for the session if Bedrock, Google Cloud's Agent Platform or Foundry refused its progress summary's effort setting (regression in 2.1.327)
  • Fixed Code Mode stopping a script when a permission prompt outside auto or bypass mode, a plan approval or a question stayed open for ten minutes
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts in auto and bypass-permissions modes failing to call an MCP server that had connected while the previous script was running
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not running in the background in auto or bypass permissions mode in a session chosen in the claude --resume picker
  • Fixed Code Mode losing a loaded skill, hook context or a note typed with a permission approval when resuming a session in which one reply ran several scripts
  • Fixed Claude not being told that a Code Mode script was cut off when the session was resumed from the picker or in a mode that asks for permission
  • Fixed Code Mode silently using undefined for top-level variables that an earlier failed script never set
  • Fixed Code Mode scripts not being told when a failing command's long output was cut
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing valid scripts that start with a { block
  • Fixed Code Mode refusing scripts that use both a top-level await and a top-level return
  • Fixed an @-mentioned small file not being attached in Code Mode after a script had read or written it
  • Fixed Code Mode offering write() and edit() to read-only subagents that can't call them
  • Fixed Claude starting a turn by itself in Code Mode when Esc was followed by a command such as /model
  • Fixed Claude in Code Mode not being told to run workflows only when you ask, or the workflow size you set in /config
  • Fixed Remote Control repeating the same disconnect message, and telling you to retry a session that can't reconnect
  • Fixed a waiting permission prompt being lost, and its answer ignored, when a remote session restarted while the service was slow
  • Fixed cloud sessions resuming a cleared conversation after a rewind followed by /clear
  • Fixed a remote session losing a turn's tool calls and results when its runner or worker was lost after a dropped model stream had been retried
  • Fixed cloud and Remote Control sessions that just started, or have an @ in their title, being unreachable in cross-session messaging from a session with Remote Control on
  • Fixed Claude being told that cloud sessions can never reply; it now learns when a reply can come and how else to get the result
  • Fixed /diff, the Changes pane of Remote Control sessions and the diff beside an edit leaving out committed work after a command moved into another repository
  • Fixed Remote Control not showing a running workflow's agents when a session run by an IDE extension or other SDK app is opened over an hour after the workflow last made progress
  • Remote Control: Fixed an idle Desktop or VS Code session showing as running after Remote Control is turned on
  • Fixed the model saying background agents were still running after an SDK interrupt had stopped them
  • Fixed Send now in the desktop app and SDK hosts telling Claude that a stopped web search found no results
  • Fixed Cmd+letter being typed into the prompt in terminals that report Cmd
  • Fixed Ctrl+click opening a link twice in GNOME Terminal, side mouse buttons acting as clicks, and the first wheel notch in the other direction being ignored after a pause, in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed Shift+Enter in Konsole outside tmux and ssh, and Alt shortcuts on non-Latin keyboard layouts in terminals that speak the kitty keyboard protocol
  • Linux: Fixed pasting in other apps freezing while Claude Code is suspended with Ctrl+Z, when xclip or wl-copy is installed
  • Linux: Fixed Ctrl+V missing the clipboard image, pasting an old one or hanging
  • Fixed text copied in fullscreen mode including the quote bar, losing spaces at line wraps when a drag scrolled upward, or missing words under the "Jump to bottom" pill
  • Fixed an image path pasted into a ! command becoming an attachment
  • Fixed Ctrl+C showing no exit warning while the ? shortcuts list is open
  • Fixed Ctrl+R search in fullscreen mode and the /theme color editor picking the wrong row when keys arrive together, and keys being dropped there and in the search of /config and /plugin
  • Fixed wrong or missing colors inside GNU screen
  • Fixed many background notifications cutting into the top border of open dialogs in fullscreen mode
  • Fixed a message to a background agent showing a long file path in place of a pasted image
  • Fixed /goal removing a skill's Stop hook, or ending early on another hook's result, when both had the same wording
  • Fixed /bug saying cancelled after the report was sent
  • Fixed Esc not dismissing the transcript share question for Pro and Max users
  • Fixed /hooks losing your place when going back
  • Fixed /export writing a file named .txt when the name was left empty
  • Fixed /terminal-setup in Zed replacing a symlinked keymap.json with a plain file
  • Fixed /install-github-app adding a code review workflow when asked to update the existing workflow file
  • Fixed /plugin reopening a skill, or closing the open page, when a slow save or removal finished after you went back
  • Fixed /plugin asking to uninstall the wrong plugin, or ignoring Esc, after leaving a plugin while a change was still running
  • Fixed typing and arrow keys not working on the /plugin Installed tab after a search with no results or a click on the tab row
  • Fixed holding Enter in /plugin turning off several installed plugins
  • Fixed the /usage plugin total stopping at 2,000 tokens on 1M context models, and low token estimates in /usage and /plugin when no model is picked
  • Fixed Esc on the Bedrock access keys step closing /login instead of going back
  • Fixed /exit and Ctrl+D describing running work differently, and /exit warning about a workflow that had stopped
  • Fixed Claude calling an artifact private after reading one in a shared folder or publishing to another organization's, and saying only named people can open one when its folder's people can too
  • Fixed a plugin's toast sometimes showing another plugin's text
  • Fixed a mod saved just after a turn began sometimes reloading mid-turn instead of at the turn's end
  • Fixed one malformed OTEL_RESOURCE_ATTRIBUTES entry dropping the variable's other labels from metric points, events, and spans. Now only that entry is left off
  • Fixed agent hooks running past their timeout while compacting after a request was refused as too large
  • Fixed a crash at startup when FORCE_COLOR is set to a negative number
  • Fixed a crash in secret masking when the machine is almost out of memory
  • Fixed the Bash sandbox on Linux renaming .git/HEAD after each command when the branch name is not valid UTF-8
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed all running sessions being stopped when a proxy or web filter answered a poll with HTTP 200 and a body such as {}; the runner now retries such a poll
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed deletion of a kept clone's objects or refs, and of commits that existed only there, after a temporary disk error; that start now fails instead
  • Fixed self-hosted runners stopping when their token ran out on a host whose clock is slow or was set back
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed sessions with Anthropic-managed git losing git access to GitHub after a script or hook in the session ran claude again
  • Fixed self-hosted runners with Anthropic-managed git being unable to fetch or push where the machine's git config sets http.proactiveAuth
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a runner that exited without telling the server when setup failed after it had registered; it now deregisters with a reason, and an on-demand runner reports the failed start
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed archiving or requeueing a session not taking effect while it waited for another session to prepare the same repository (--capacity above 1)
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session with a damaged .claude.json failing every later start under --trust-workspace false; it now starts on defaults, with MCP servers turned off there on again
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a failed start's message losing the words that say what failed when a checkout hook or git printed a lot
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner skipping its post-session hook when a disk stalled for a few seconds; on a dead disk a session's end can take 25 seconds longer by default
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: a session that resumes in a new Claude config directory no longer loses its task list
  • Fixed Claude not being told when a self-hosted session starts without one of its repositories, and why
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed --correlation-id of claude --environment not reaching the spawn-runner hook
  • Fixed the self-hosted runner setup wizard's key rotation advice, which now warns that revoking a key stops the sessions running under it
  • Improved claude -p and SDK sessions to fetch managed-settings plugins that have their own git repository, in the background, for a later session
  • Improved how soon managed-settings plugins from a git marketplace load on a fresh machine in claude -p, SDK and Claude Desktop sessions; a short run may exit up to 30 seconds later
  • Improved the time to resume large sessions
  • Improved memory use when resuming a session with many images
  • Improved memory use and response time in long SDK and desktop sessions that run slow commands or tools
  • Improved Code Mode's speed in auto and bypass-permissions modes by removing a 0.75 second pause after most scripts
  • Improved prompt caching for new Code Mode sessions that have MCP servers, and Claude is now told when a server is still connecting and when the list of servers changes
  • Improved Code Mode's token use with shorter tool descriptions
  • Improved Code Mode to show the command a script is running, and its output, while it runs
  • Improved Code Mode edits: an edit that changes nothing no longer stops a script, and Claude is told where a failed edit matches or comes closest
  • Improved Code Mode: Claude is now told which tool calls were still running when a script failed
  • Improved how Claude starts dev servers in Code Mode's auto and bypass modes: Claude is told to run them as background tasks that show in /tasks
  • Windows: Improved Code Mode by telling Claude that scripts' shell commands run in Git Bash and that PowerShell aliases run instead of functions with the same name
  • Improved starting several in-process teammates at once: far fewer now fail with "Lock file is already being held"
  • Improved the computer use approval dialog: it now shows each app's level of access and plainer warnings
  • Improved cross-session messaging: Claude now explains that Remote Control is off when a cloud session or another computer is not listed
  • Improved claude -p text output to say on stderr when a message from another session is held or dropped, and how to allow it
  • Improved Claude's answers on who can open an artifact it published: Claude is now told to check the artifact again instead of repeating the last publish's answer
  • Improved resumed self-hosted runner sessions: Claude now checks whether its earlier work is still there, and says what is missing
  • Changed plan mode and Bash prompts for Opus 4.6 and Sonnet 4.6 on third-party providers to use and offer auto mode, as on newer models; disableAutoMode turns both off
  • Changed Code Mode to no longer run UserPromptSubmit hooks, managed ones included, on scripts' output; to redact that output, use a PostToolUse hook with updatedToolOutput
  • Changed /code-review on most models to report only bugs and CLAUDE.md violations; run /simplify for reuse, simplification and efficiency cleanups
  • Changed /code-review to mark each finding Important, Pre-existing or Nit on most models, and to end each summary with a suggested fix; a clean review's list now reads "Code review found no issues."
  • Changed deniedMcpServers entries of the form claude.ai <name> to apply to that connector in cloud and self-hosted runner sessions too
  • Changed managed PostToolUse hooks to no longer fire for calls refused before they ran: no log entry, rewrite, block or stop there; PostToolBatch gets most, not marked as refused
  • Changed /bug to ask Yes or No before sending, so repeated Enters no longer send a report or open GitHub
  • Changed subagents in claude -p, the Agent SDK, desktop and VS Code to wait for their own subagents by default when CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 is set
  • Changed claude -p with CLAUDE_CODE_FORK_SUBAGENT=0 to count a background subagent and those it waits for against one 10-minute wait; raise CLAUDE_CODE_PRINT_BG_WAIT_CEILING_MS for longer chains
  • Changed a shell command rewritten by a PermissionRequest hook to a sandbox-excluded command to run outside the sandbox
  • Changed the Claude in Chrome welcome screen and /chrome to say that Claude Code asks before Claude acts on a site, unless your permission mode or a rule in /permissions answers
  • Changed Claude Desktop and Agent SDK sessions on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags off to end the turn when closed with a question open, instead of continuing without an answer
  • Changed pasted text to be marked for Claude as pasted, on third-party providers or with telemetry or feature flags turned off
  • Changed subagent progress summaries in terminal sessions on the Anthropic API to be written by the default small fast model from short notes, also with telemetry off, using far fewer tokens
  • Changed how a sandbox that can't start is reported, unless sandbox.failIfUnavailable is set: the next sandboxed Bash command is refused and says that the sandbox is off for the session
  • Changed /list-agents to show its list to you alone; Claude lists sessions itself when needed
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed the built-in gh api to be off by default where settings guard Claude's GitHub tools by name; --use-anthropic-gh true turns it on
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed a claude that a wrapper script runs before the session's own claude is up, or after it has ended, to have no Anthropic-managed git
  • Self-hosted runner: Changed CLAUDE_RUNNER_SESSION_UUID and CLAUDE_CODE_REMOTE_SESSION_UUID to both be set for the session and its checkout, post-session and spawn-runner hooks
  • Changed self-hosted runners at --capacity 1 to refuse a session earlier when the path of a repository it pushes to is a symbolic link
  • [VSCode] Added a notice when a message from another session is held, with a link to the settings file that can allow it
  • [VSCode] Fixed the permission prompt cutting off its No button, reply field or title when the panel is low or a command, URL or description is long
  • [VSCode] Fixed failed or blocked tool calls showing no reason or a reason cut short, and Glob and Grep counting an error as results
